text: tornado diagram shown in Figure 40 illustrates the results of a sensitivity study on LCOC for the DAC system. The red arrow simplifies the direction of increase of the studied parameter. The analysis evaluates the influence of key technical and economic parameters by varying each within the specified uncertainty ranges while holding the others constant. Among the parameters, total plant cost emerges as the dominant driver of LCOC, producing the widest variation in capture cost. This indicates that capital investment exerts the strongest leverage on project economics and highlights the importance of accurate cost estimation in early- stage project assessment. Sorbent regeneration electricity also has a significant impact, shifting the capture cost by nearly ±$40–60 per tonne of CO₂. This TEA assumes an inlet air concentration of 328 ppm CO₂. If actual site conditions provide slightly higher CO₂ concentrations, production would increase, and the overall capture cost would decline. Conversely, even a small decrease in concentration—while keeping all other equipment and operating parameters unchanged—would reduce production and noticeably raise the capture cost. These results highlight the dual importance of process energy efficiency and site-specific CO₂ concentrations in determining the overall feasibility of DAC deployment. By contrast, parameters such as sorbent cost, mat lifetime, and adsorption fan pressure drop display comparatively smaller effects on the LCOC within the studied ranges. While these factors should not be neglected, their economic weight is less critical than capital expenditure and energy requirements. 47 4. Summary and Future Steps An innovative sorbent structure of trapped small amines in HNC embedded in PEF was developed for DAC. This involves tailoring both sorbent and PEF materials to achieve a compact system for DAC with high capacity for CO at concentrations typically available in air and at near 2 ambient conditions. An interfacial polymerization process was developed, which utilized loaded amines inside mesoporous silica and TMC dissolved in organic solvents as the precursors, to generate a PA coating layer on mesoporous silica and thus trap amines. Reaction conditions for interfacial polymerization were optimized to effectively trap loaded amines, and cyclic heating- cooling operation was conducted to evaluate the coating quality. Larger pore volume mesoporous silica was also synthesized to increase amine loading and thus increase CO capacity. 2 The optimized sorbent material exhibited CO capacity as high as 4.88 mmol/g under humid 2 DAC conditions and negligible loss (<1%) during 10 cyclic heating-cooling operations. The optimized PA-coated sorbent also showed fast adsorption and desorption kinetics, with <20% t 1/2 increase compared to uncoated sorbent. PEF fabrication conditions were adjusted to better incorporate HNC. After incorporating the optimized sorbent material into PEF, the structured sorbent had a CO capacity of approximately 4.0 mmol/g under humid DAC conditions, with 2 capacity loss of 0.17% per cycle and t increase less than 10%. 1/2 TEA for the process design for a DAC system based on our developed sorbent structure of trapped small amines in HNC embedded in PEF was conducted.
